title: Bharat Biotech Cuts Malaria Vaccine Price 40% in Gavi-UNICEF Deal
excerpt: Mosqivac will fall to €5.50 a dose from early 2027, saving programmes about $50 million and funding full courses for up to a million more children.
body:
• Bharat Biotech's malaria vaccine Mosqivac will cost €5.50 per dose under a Gavi-UNICEF agreement — a cut of about 40% from the current €9.30.
  • The lower price, effective from early 2027, is expected to save immunisation programmes about $50 million between 2027 and 2029 and fund full four-dose courses for up to one million more children.
  • Mosqivac is the RTS,S/AS01 vaccine developed by GSK and PATH — the first malaria vaccine the WHO recommended, in 2021 — now manufactured by Hyderabad-based Bharat Biotech.
  • The cut is enabled by an advance payment through the International Finance Facility for Immunisation and $200 million invested by GSK and Bharat Biotech in higher-output manufacturing.

Bharat Biotech has agreed an equitable pricing deal with Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, and UNICEF that will cut the price of the world's first malaria vaccine by about 40 per cent, to €5.50 per dose. The agreement, executed by UNICEF and financially backed by Gavi, is expected to generate around $50 million in savings for child immunisation programmes between 2027 and 2029 and reach up to one million more children with the full four-dose course, according to The Hindu BusinessLine.

How the price falls

The mechanism is advance financing: an advance payment by the International Finance Facility for Immunisation (IFFIm) lets UNICEF lock in the lower price, which takes effect by early 2027. Behind it sits a manufacturing bet — since the vaccine's WHO recommendation in 2021, GSK and Bharat Biotech have invested $200 million in new, higher-output facilities, product development and technology transfer so the vaccine can be made at greater volume and lower cost. Bharat Biotech manufactures the vaccine, developed by GSK with PATH and partners, under the brand name Mosqivac; GSK continues to supply the adjuvant component as production transfers fully to the Indian company by 2028.

"The Gavi-UNICEF deal is a far-reaching commitment to expand malaria vaccination and according to Gavi/UNICEF estimates, can help ensure one million more children are protected from malaria."

— Dr Krishna Ella, Executive Chairman, Bharat Biotech

Why the price matters in absolute terms

A four-dose course is what protects a child, so the per-dose cut compounds: at €5.50 instead of about €9.30, a full course costs roughly €22 rather than €37 — the arithmetic behind the estimate that the same programme budgets can cover up to a million additional children, as Express Pharma reported. The agreement is subject to regulatory and manufacturing milestones, including WHO prequalification of the new manufacturing facility, before UNICEF procurement at the new price begins.

What happens next

The lower price takes effect in early 2027, with savings counted across 2027-2029. GSK and Bharat Biotech have previously said they aim to bring the price below $5 per dose by 2028 as the technology transfer completes. For malaria-endemic countries deciding whether to introduce the vaccine into routine immunisation, the commitment converts a pilot-stage product into something a national budget can plan around — and puts an Indian manufacturer at the centre of the supply chain for a disease that still kills hundreds of thousands of children a year, most of them in Africa.
